text: Given the prodrome of fever, rhinorrhea, and headache followed by a spreading pruritic rash, this clinical picture is highly suggestive of a viral exanthem, such as rubella or a non-specific viral rash. speaker: Doctor
text: The presence of postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy strongly points toward rubella. Do you have any joint pain or stiffness, particularly in your hands or wrists?

speaker: Doctor
text: Since you lack joint pain, which is common in adult rubella, I need to rule out other causes like roseola or an atypical measles presentation. Have you received a measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine in the past, or do you have any known allergies to medications?

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your vaccination history, rubella is less likely, so I need to consider other viral exanthems like roseola or enterovirus. Did you notice any rash on your face before it spread to your trunk, and have you experienced any cough or conjunctivitis?

speaker: Doctor
text: The facial rash sparing the perioral area combined with your symptoms is highly characteristic of Erythema Infectiosum, also known as Fifth Disease. To confirm this diagnosis, can you tell me if the rash on your trunk and extremities has a lacy or reticular appearance?

speaker: Patient
text: Yes, the rash on my body looks like a lacy or net-like pattern. It seems to fade and then reappear, especially when I change temperatures.

speaker: Doctor
text: The lacy, reticular rash that fades and reappears with temperature changes is pathognomonic for Erythema Infectiosum, also known as Fifth Disease, caused by Parvovirus B19. DIAGNOSIS READY: Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth Disease)
